query: What signals in a travel-expense description predict whether it will be declined?

per_column.name: asset_category_type
per_column.rationale: Well-separated, interpretable categories (hardware_device, travel_equipment, cloud_service, etc.) that a human can group on and compare decline rates across. External to the focus and associational.

per_column.name: asset_purpose_signal
per_column.rationale: Interpretable purpose categories with reasonable spread; supports segmentation of declines by purpose. Overlaps somewhat with asset_category_type but adds a distinct purpose framing.

per_column.name: expense_source_indicator
per_column.rationale: Clear, distinguishable origin categories (procurement, automated_creation, travel_related, etc.) that plausibly relate to decline likelihood and can be compared as segments.

per_column.name: departmental_context
per_column.rationale: Interpretable categories, but the original table already contains a 'department' column; this largely restates existing data rather than opening a new associational axis.

per_column.name: source_system_origin
per_column.rationale: Only three clean, well-separated categories (internal_ticket_system, asset_management_system, expense_system) that segment well and can reveal system-level differences in decline rates.

judge.rationale: The set provides mostly interpretable, well-separated categorical variables external to the focus, each groupable for comparing decline rates -- satisfying the EDA claim. However there is notable redundancy: asset_category_type / asset_purpose_signal / expense_source_indicator overlap conceptually (all encode a 'travel_related' vs equipment/service distinction), and departmental_context duplicates the existing 'department' column, restating rather than extending the data. No opaque scores are present, which is good, but the redundancy limits the breadth of distinct relationships a human explorer can discover around state_declined.
